pages.introduction: This section has standards and specifications for defining Trailhead content, including trails and various types of badges.

guidelines: A new trail format was launched at Dreamforce 2024: enhanced trails (informally known as trails 2.0).
Enhanced trail: 1-7 milestones with 2-7 steps in each milestone

Note: A badge can be included in multiple trails. A public trail contains only public badges, but an employee trail can contain both public and employee badges. (Both public and private badges can be added to a private trailmix.)
1500 is the maximum number of words per unit, but limiting to 500-1000 words is strongly recommended because badge completion rates are lower on longer content.
* You may exclude the words in image alt text, code snippets, interactivities, resources, and quizzes from the word count.

pages.introduction: Follow these guidelines as you write titles and descriptions for your content.
pages.note: Use "General" only when no other product value applies.

guidelines.structure: [imperative verb] + [topic], No more than 80 characters, Title capitalization

Automate Your Business Processes with Lightning Flow

pages.introduction: Also known as tags, filters help Trailblazers find relevant badges and trails by product/feature, role, skill, industry, and level of experience.
product_fields: The Trailhead Product Categories field reflects one or more values that you specify in the Trailhead Products/Features field.

The Trailhead Products/Features field (formerly Trailhead Product Filter) allows you to specify one or more products/features that Trailblazers can select on Trailhead to see content related to those products/features.
The Primary Product/Feature field (formerly Primary Product) allows you to specify the product/feature most prominently featured in the badge, for internal reporting purposes.
pages.note: Trails inherit Trailhead Product Category and Trailhead Products/Features from the badges in the trail.
pages.reference_link: See the latest product tags available in GUS/Trailhead UI here.
best_practices: Usually you only need one product/feature tag. There might be some exceptions for products/features that overlap, such as Lightning. For example, Lightning Web Components Basics has two product tags: Lightning and Agentforce 360 Platform.
Avoid using General/No Salesforce Product if possible. (Choose General/No Salesforce Product only if no other product fits.)
Never use General/No Salesforce Product along with another product.

Use General/No Salesforce Product if the badge is: Not related to a Salesforce product or feature or industry (e.g., Git and Github Basics); Related to a product that doesn't have a product tag yet (e.g., myTrailhead Basics); About soft skills (e.g., Writing Style).

pages.introduction: Also known as tags, filters help Trailblazers find relevant badges and trails by product/feature, role, skill, industry, and level of experience.
pages.badge_focus: Each Trailhead badge should be focused on a specific target audience. When you create a badge, you've got to know your audience.
audience_questions: Who is the learner? An admin, a designer, a marketer, a student?
What's their level of experience with the subject? Beginner, intermediate, or advanced?
What are their goals? Get started, address pain points, learn about new features?

roles.note: Choose only one role for a badge.

role_definitions.description: A Salesforce Administrator configures and manages the Agentforce 360 Platform, ensuring that it meets the company's requirements. They handle user accounts, create reports, dashboards, workflows, and maintain data quality.

A Salesforce Architect designs scalable and robust solutions within the Agentforce 360 Platform. They are responsible for the overall structure of Salesforce systems, ensuring they align with business processes and technical requirements.

A Salesforce Business Analyst acts as a bridge between business problems and technology solutions. They analyze business processes, gather requirements, and help design Salesforce solutions that improve efficiency and productivity.

A Salesforce Consultant advises businesses on how to best use the Agentforce 360 Platform. They analyze business needs, recommend solutions, and help implement Salesforce systems to meet strategic objectives.

A Customer Service Professional uses Salesforce Service Cloud to manage customer support and service processes. They handle customer inquiries, cases, and provide support to ensure a high level of customer satisfaction.

A professional focused on Cybersecurity within Salesforce is responsible for securing the Salesforce environment. This includes safeguarding sensitive data, monitoring for security threats, and ensuring compliance with security policies and regulations.
A Data Analyst enables stakeholders to make business decisions by understanding the business problem, identifying data to explore for analysis, and delivering actionable insights.

A Salesforce Designer focuses on the user interface and experience within the Agentforce 360 Platform. They design the layout, visual elements, and interactions to ensure a seamless and effective user experience.

A Salesforce Developer builds and customizes Salesforce applications using the platform's various development tools, such as Apex, Visualforce, and Lightning Components. They write code to create new functionality and integrate external systems.
An End User is an individual who uses Salesforce on a daily basis to perform their job functions and achieve the business goals and objectives.
A Marketer in the Salesforce ecosystem uses Salesforce Marketing Cloud and other marketing tools to create and manage marketing campaigns, track customer journeys, and analyze marketing performance.
A Sales Professional uses Salesforce Sales Cloud to manage their sales processes, including tracking leads, opportunities, and customer interactions, to close deals and grow revenue.

roles.general_skills_note: For general information and soft skills (such as public speaking skills or Trailhead basics), choose the End User role.

levels.description: Use these level descriptions to understand what your target audience knows and can do. Then you can create content that's appropriate for their role and skill level.

level_definitions.user_facing_definition: Are you ready to start your Salesforce journey or explore the latest product features and industry trends? This content is tailored for both new Trailblazers and experienced professionals. You're introduced to Salesforce products and features, essential skills, and industry tools, all while preparing for foundational-level certifications. Discover various roles within the Salesforce ecosystem and stay up-to-date on key industry themes and technologies.
level_definitions.target_audience: New Salesforce users, beginners, or individuals with limited or no prior experience in Salesforce.
learning_focus: Prepares for foundational level certifications
Introduces basic product features or terminology
Provides a foundational understanding of Salesforce products, skills, navigation, and/or concepts
Introduces Salesforce roles and essential skills
Covers key industry themes, trends, and technologies
Helps learners transition from an outside platform to Salesforce, such as 'SQL to SOQL'
Focuses on both click and code skills

level_definitions.user_facing_definition: Ready to take your Salesforce skills to the next level? This content is for those with some experience who want to deepen their understanding and proficiency in specific Salesforce roles or products. Build on your basics and showcase your growing expertise!
level_definitions.target_audience: Users with a working knowledge of Salesforce that are exploring new products and features to handle more complex organizational needs. Intermediate learners have moved beyond the basics and are now delving deeper into specific areas of the Agentforce 360 Platform. They are building on their foundational knowledge and starting to apply what they have learned in more complex scenarios.
learning_focus: Prepares for Professional certifications
Covers core elements of setup and implementation
Teaches learners to tailor Salesforce solutions for their business
Engages in discovery to grasp customer requirements
Shares best practices to design basic Salesforce solutions
Delves into industry-specific themes, trends, and tech discussions
Teaches the learner how to do all types of testing for code and click solutions
Supports and troubleshoots user challenges

level_definitions.user_facing_definition: Elevate your Salesforce expertise! Designed for professionals familiar with the basics, this content helps you tackle more complex tasks and challenges within the Salesforce ecosystem. Enhance your skills and become a Salesforce pro by optimizing and expanding your use of Salesforce!
level_definitions.target_audience: Experienced Salesforce users, consultants, developers, and admins, including those working toward specialist certifications. They are capable of handling complex tasks and are often seen as experts within their organizations.
learning_focus: Prepares for Advanced certifications
Deepens expertise in Salesforce configuration, usage, and complex feature applications
Expands knowledge with multi-cloud solutions and integrates them into business ecosystems
Delves into complex automation

Analyzes industry trends for strategic application and elevates digital transformations with advanced strategies

pages.introduction: Also known as tags, filters help Trailblazers find relevant badges and trails. The Industries filter on Trailhead relies on Industry tags in metadata to associate the badge with relevant business domain(s). Not every Trailhead badge needs to be tagged with an Industry, but badges where the tags do apply will benefit from better discoverability.

sections.section_title: Where does the list of Industry tags come from?
sections.content: Industry tags align with the L1 Industries listed in the Salesforce C360 taxonomy. In turn, the C360 Industries categories map to Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, which are governed by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

sections.section_title: What Industry tags are available on Trailhead?
How do I determine which Industry filter(s) to use for my badge?
sections.approach: Employ a structured approach combining direct product-to-industry mapping with a criteria-based approach to refine tagging for products spanning multiple industries.
sections.note: Select at least one, and no more than five tags per badge to ensure meaningful results overall. The only exceptions are Industries common components such as Contract and Document Generation, Business Rules Engine (BRE), and Omnistudio, which may have up to eight tags.

subsections.description: Several products map directly to an Industry tag.

subsections.subsection_title: Criteria for Cross-Cloud Industry Mapping and Refinement
subsections.guiding_question: What are the priority Industries where we want this content to be discoverable using the filter on Trailhead?
subsections.approach: Initially, align the product covered in the badge with the broadest applicable industry category. Further refine the badge's alignment by identifying more specific sectors or niches within the broad industry category that the content directly addresses. This structured approach ensures that badges are categorized in a way that reflects both their broad industry relevance and their applicability to specific sectors.
steps: Familiarize yourself with the available Industry tags and how they are defined: Refer to the list of tags above (or the Industry field pick list in a GUS badge record). See the Definitions table in the section below for more context about the business domain encompassed by each tag.
Analyze badge content: Evaluate the badge's description, learning objectives, target role, and associated skills to align with the appropriate Industry tags.

Collaborate for accuracy: Confer with your manager or strategist to choose the best tag(s) based on badge content and goals. Remember, select at least one, and no more than five tags per badge to ensure meaningful results overall.

example.badge_description: Build out your catalog offerings faster and more precisely.
process: The writer knows from content planning conversations that direct product-to-industry mapping does not apply for this badge.
The writer confers with the content strategist on their team, and together they determine that Enterprise Product Catalog (EPC) is the appropriate internal Primary Product tag.

The writer cross references the badge description, learning objectives, and the associated roles and skills to further refine the alignment with Industry tags. They also scan the Industry tags of badges in this same content area.
Based on this research and analysis, the writer proposes to their editor and content strategist that the Industry tags for this badge are Communications and Media and Energy and Utilities.

sections.section_title: How are the Industry tags on Trailhead defined?

definitions.definition: Agriculture: The production of crops, plants, vines, or trees; and the keeping, grazing, or feeding of livestock. Mining: The extraction of minerals occurring naturally: solids, such as coal and ores; liquids, such as crude petroleum; and gases such as natural gas.

Communications: Furnishing point-to-point communications services, whether intended to be received aurally or visually; and radio and television broadcasting. Media: Preparing advertising and support materials (writing copy, artwork, graphics, and other creative work) and placing in periodicals, newspapers, radio and television, or other media.
Providing academic or technical instruction. Also includes libraries, student exchange programs, and curriculum development.

The generation, transmission, and/or distribution of electricity or gas or steam. Water and irrigation systems, and sanitary systems engaged in the collection and disposal of garbage, sewage, and other wastes by means of destroying or processing materials.

Engineering: Industrial, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering services. Construction: Building construction and heavy construction resulting in new work, additions, alterations, reconstruction, installations, and repairs. Real Estate: Real estate operators, and owners and lessors of real property, as well as buyers, sellers, developers, reps, and brokers.
Depository institutions, non-depository credit institutions, holding and other investment companies, brokers and dealers in securities and commodity contracts, and security and commodity exchanges.

Health services provided to individuals. These services can occur in a variety of work settings, including hospitals, clinics, dental offices, out-patient surgery centers, birthing centers, emergency medical care, home healthcare, and nursing homes.
Computer programming services such as computer software design and analysis; modifications of custom software; and training in the use of custom software.

Manufacturing: The mechanical or chemical transformation of materials or substances into new products. Automotive: Retail dealers selling new and used automobiles, boats, recreational vehicles, utility trailers, and motorcycles.
Non-governmental organizations primarily engaged in providing social services, including community improvement and social change, or other mission-based work such as animal welfare organizations.

Providing a wide variety of services for individuals, business and government establishments, and other organizations. Includes personal, business, repair, and amusement services, and membership organizations.
The executive, legislative, judicial, administrative and regulatory activities of Federal, State, local, and international governments.
Selling merchandise for personal or household consumption and rendering services incidental to the sale of the goods.

Travel: Furnishing travel information and acting as reps in arranging tours, transportation, rental of cars, and lodging for travelers. Transportation: Passenger and freight transportation provided to the general public or to other business enterprises. Hospitality: Lodging, or lodging and meals, provided for the general public.

sections.section_title: Requesting changes to the Trailhead Taxonomy
sections.content: The Content Strategy Team will review Trailhead skills taxonomy and make revisions as needed to ensure learners can find the most in-demand skills on Trailhead. The Taxonomy will be reviewed on an ad-hoc basis as new quests are made and when new skills research is released. To learn more review the Trailhead Skills Taxonomy Change Process.
